reels.title: The Done Trap

scenes.narration: Your coding agent saying done proves almost nothing. One green line can quietly hide a failed test, a red console, and a deployment that broke ten minutes earlier.
scenes.concept: Giant green confirmation, then the camera pulls back.

scenes.narration: Pull the camera back and the truth appears beside it: the test failed, the console is full of errors, and the deploy is warning you about config.
scenes.concept: Hidden failures appear behind the confirmation card.

scenes.narration: So build a real pipeline instead: tests first, then logs, then actual browser behaviour, and finally a human or independent review, in that order, every time.
scenes.concept: Four verification stages connect left to right.

scenes.narration: Each stage runs, one of them fails, the agent patches the cause, and the whole pipeline starts again from the very top until everything agrees.
scenes.concept: One failing assertion highlights, then the fix lands.

visual.label: VERIFICATION
visual.note: Failure is information, not a verdict.

scenes.narration: Only when all four pass should the word done come back into the output. Completion is agreement between evidence and claim, never a confident sentence on its own.
scenes.concept: All four stages green, confirmation returns.

visual.label: STANDARD
visual.a: Tests · Logs · Browser · Review — all green.

reels.title: Most AI Coding Setups Are Backwards

scenes.text: Upgrading the model is the wrong upgrade.
scenes.narration: Most people upgrade the model first, and that is usually the wrong upgrade, because the model is only ever one layer of the system around it.
scenes.concept: Model chip upgrades twice; the output gauge barely moves.

scenes.narration: Pull the camera back and you find five layers sitting underneath: effort, context, skills, tools, and verification, each one doing work the model never sees.
scenes.concept: Stack diagram reveals the layers beneath the model.

scenes.narration: Fill the first three quickly: set the effort dial to match the task, write the project rules to disk, and turn everything you repeat into reusable skills.
scenes.concept: Three layers fill in sequence with the spoken line.

scenes.narration: Then connect the tools the agent actually needs, and make it run the tests before it is allowed to claim anything at all about the work.
scenes.concept: Project file docks, then the test command executes.

visual.label: PROJECT RULES
visual.note: Rules persist instead of being retyped.

scenes.narration: The model is only one layer of the stack. Context, tools, and proof are what make it genuinely useful inside a real repository with real consequences.

visual.label: THE UPGRADE
visual.a: Improve the system around the model, not just the model.

reels.title: You’re Probably Using the Wrong Effort Level

scenes.narration: Max reasoning is not the best setting for every coding task.

scenes.text: One-line diff next to huge reasoning animation.
scenes.narration: Turning it on permanently feels safe and quietly costs you time and tokens. Renaming a button does not need a wall of reasoning animation.

scenes.narration: Match the effort to the task instead of leaving one dial stuck on maximum. A rename belongs on low, a feature belongs somewhere in the middle. A bug hunt across hidden edge cases earns the higher setting.

scenes.text: Bug branches multiply under a code card.
scenes.narration: A security review earns the full budget, because being wrong there is expensive. Higher effort helps where the answer is not already obvious in the diff. It will not save a task you described badly.

reels.title: `CLAUDE.md` Is Better Than Repeating Yourself

scenes.narration: If you explain your project rules in every chat, your setup is broken.
The same build command, the same folder rules, pasted for the fifth time. Repetition does not make the model smarter, it just makes the context longer.

scenes.text: Code editor creates a clean project file.
scenes.narration: So move the rules into a file the project owns. Write them once, and every new session reads them before it writes anything. Duplicate lines stop flashing, and the prompt shrinks to the actual task.

visual.label: CODE EDITOR CREATES
visual.note: Code editor creates a clean project file.

scenes.text: New terminal opens; chips dock automatically.
scenes.narration: A fresh terminal opens with the context already docked in place. Compare forty lines of history against one line of intent. Persistent instructions beat repeated explanations every single time.

visual.label: NEW TERMINAL OPENS
code: // the rules appear as compact context chips.
visual.note: New terminal opens; chips dock automatically.

scenes.text: Split screen collapses to simple task prompt.
scenes.narration: Explain the project once, then spend the conversation on the work. Write the rules once in a file and let every session inherit them.

visual.label: SPLIT SCREEN COLLAPSES

visual.note: Split screen collapses to simple task prompt.

reels.title: Give Your AI Coder Eyes and Hands

scenes.narration: Pasting screenshots into your coding agent is the slow version of context.

scenes.text: Agent node in center; disconnected nodes around it.
scenes.narration: A blurry image and the question why is this broken, typed by hand. The agent guesses from a picture because nobody gave it a door.

visual.label: AGENT NODE IN
visual.note: Agent node in center; disconnected nodes around it.

scenes.narration: Pull the camera back and the agent sits alone in the middle. Database, deployment logs and browser tools all live outside the conversation. Connect them with cables and the agent can read instead of imagine. It inspects the table, reads the error, checks the deployment state.

scenes.text: Fast UI zooms inside each node.
scenes.narration: Each node pulses, and the screenshot quietly leaves the chat. Real systems beat reconstructed guesses every single time. Context you can query always outperforms context you pasted.

visual.label: FAST UI ZOOMS
visual.note: Fast UI zooms inside each node.

scenes.text: All nodes pulse together; screenshot is discarded.
scenes.narration: Give the model eyes and hands rather than a photograph of both. Better context beats better guessing, and it starts with the connection.

visual.label: ALL NODES PULSE
visual.note: All nodes pulse together; screenshot is discarded.

reels.title: Two Models, One Pull Request

scenes.narration: The easiest way to make an AI coder less overconfident is to give it an opponent.
One agent approving its own code is a rubber stamp with extra steps. Split the screen: builder on the left, reviewer on the right.

The builder writes the diff and the reviewer reads it with a different job. Security, tests and edge cases get flagged by someone who did not write them. The builder patches, the reviewer re-runs, and the counter falls.
Independent review is the point, not the second logo. Two models only help when the second one is allowed to disagree. If it just agrees politely, you paid for a mirror.

scenes.text: Two agents collapse into BUILD ↔ REVIEW loop.
scenes.narration: Give the reviewer a role and a reason to reject the change. Then the pull request survives contact with production.

visual.label: TWO AGENTS COLLAPSE
visual.note: Two agents collapse into BUILD ↔ REVIEW loop.

reels.title: Make Claude and Codex Argue Until the Code Survives

scenes.narration: What if the second AI was paid to disagree with the first?
Code sits between two panels, one labelled claim, the other challenge. The first agent writes the plan and states its assumptions out loud.

scenes.text: Red challenge cards hit the plan.
scenes.narration: The second one attacks them: authentication, race conditions, bad input. Every challenge card either gets fixed or gets proved wrong. Defending with evidence means tests, not confidence.

visual.label: RED CHALLENGE CARDS
visual.note: Red challenge cards hit the plan.

scenes.narration: The counter drops from five objections down to zero. Only then does the merge button unlock. Turn multi-model review into an argument, not a duplicate.

visual.label: CARDS SWITCH TO
code: // Agent A must either fix or defend every

scenes.narration: Two agents that agree are one agent with extra compute. Adversarial review finds the edge case your first pass already liked. Ship when the disagreement reaches zero, and not one commit earlier. Ship only when the second model has run out of objections.

reels.title: Stop Copy-Pasting the Same Giant Prompt

scenes.narration: If your best prompt is two hundred lines long, it has become a workflow.
Pasting it again is not prompting; it is re-implementing your own tooling. Watch the sections scroll past: plan, code, test, review.
Colour the borders and the repetition becomes obvious. Cut those sections into modular cards you can invoke by name. One card for planning, one for building, one for testing, one for review.
Call a single card on a new task and the stored procedure runs. The prompt folds, the modules dock, and nothing has to be retyped. Prompts describe; workflows repeat.

visual.label: TERMINAL COMMAND MINI
items: Invoke one card on a new task

scenes.text: Prompt sheet folds into reusable modules.
scenes.narration: Repetition is a signal that something should already be code. Turn the giant paste into a command and stop paying for it daily. Turn the paste into a command and stop paying for it every time.

visual.label: PROMPT SHEET FOLDS
items: Prompt sheet folds into reusable modules.
visual.note: Prompt sheet folds into reusable modules.

reels.title: What a Good AI Coding Plugin Actually Adds

scenes.narration: A plugin that only adds another prompt is barely a plugin.
Installed, and behind it sits one more text file. Judge it by the sockets it fills, not by the install count.

scenes.text: Skill = review checklist; agent = specialist; hook =
scenes.narration: Skills hold reusable instructions and checklists the agent can pull. Agents add specialists with their own scope and tools. Hooks fire after an edit, running tests before anything ships. Connections reach external systems that the model cannot touch alone.

visual.label: SKILL REVIEW CHECKLIST
visual.note: Skill = review checklist; agent = specialist; hook = post-edit

scenes.narration: Fill those four sockets with real examples and the plugin earns its place. Run one task and watch them fire in sequence. Instructions, agents, hooks, tools, in that order down the board.
Anything beyond that is decoration with a version number. Judge plugins by what they automate, not by what they promise. Four working sockets beat four paragraphs of documentation any day.

reels.title: Your Browser Is Better Debug Context Than a Screenshot

scenes.narration: A screenshot shows the symptom; DevTools shows the cause.

scenes.text: Image zooms; almost no technical data.
scenes.narration: The broken checkout image tells you almost nothing technical. Ask what you can actually learn from it and the answer is colour.

visual.label: IMAGE ZOOMS ALMOST
visual.note: Image zooms; almost no technical data.

scenes.narration: Open the console and the first real sentence appears. Follow the failed network request, then the stack trace underneath it. Trace the request id back to the exact line that produced it. Console, network and performance are context a photograph can never carry.

visual.label: BROWSER PANELS SLIDE
visual.a: Open DevTools: console error → failed network request →

scenes.text: Animated connection from request ID to editor line.
scenes.narration: Give the agent that instead of a picture of a red toast. It reads the error, finds the handler, and writes the fix. Reload, watch the row turn two hundred, and the checkout succeeds.

scenes.narration: Symptoms get pasted; causes get inspected. So hand over the browser, not the crop. Hand the agent the console and the network tab, not the crop.

reels.title: Let the Agent Read Your Deployment Logs

scenes.narration: Your code can be correct and your deployment can still be broken.
It works on your machine, and production answers with a five hundred. Deployment logs are part of the debugging loop, not a last resort.

Expand the deployment timeline and isolate the failed build step. Let the agent read the environment variables, the config, the build output. Then it patches the real cause instead of guessing at the code.

Re-deploy, watch the progress bar complete, and check both cards. Local green and production green at the same time is the actual finish line. Most agent failures are context failures wearing a different hat.
Read the logs first and the fix is usually obvious. Debug the system, not just the file you were editing. Read the deployment before you blame the code you already wrote.

reels.title: Let the Agent Query the Database — But Not Production Blindly

scenes.narration: Database access makes an AI coder powerful; production write access makes it dangerous.
A giant red button labelled drop, migrate or delete is not a tool call. Scope the permissions into lanes before you hand anything over.

Read everywhere, write in staging, and keep production approval locked. Inspecting the schema and running a select is safe and useful. Generating the migration in staging lets the tests speak first. If they pass, a human approves the last step.

visual.label: TABLE BROWSER SQL
visual.a: Agent inspects schema and runs a read query safely.

scenes.text: Staging card green; prod lock icon.
scenes.narration: Destructive actions should require confirmation, never momentum. Tool access needs boundaries, not trust. Trust is what you extend after the boundary already worked.

visual.label: STAGING CARD GREEN
visual.note: Staging card green; prod lock icon.

scenes.narration: Broad inspection gives the agent context; narrow writes keep the data alive. That asymmetry is the whole safety model. Inspect broadly, write narrowly, and require a human for the dangerous call.

reels.title: The Hidden Prompt Is Part of the Product

scenes.narration: The model is only half the behaviour you are talking to.

scenes.text: Layers labelled SYSTEM / TOOLS / MEMORY / POLICY.
scenes.narration: Your request is one line; the scaffold behind it is enormous. System instructions, tool definitions, memory and policy all shape the reply.

visual.label: LAYERS LABELLED SYSTEM
items: a huge hidden scaffold appears behind it.
visual.note: Layers labelled SYSTEM / TOOLS / MEMORY / POLICY.

scenes.text: Animated prompt packet travels through stack.
scenes.narration: Pull the camera back and the hidden stack appears. The same prompt routes through every layer before anyone sees an answer. Remove the tools and the capability disappears entirely. Remove the instructions and the behaviour changes without the model changing.

visual.label: ANIMATED PROMPT PACKET
code: // Animated prompt packet travels through stack.

scenes.narration: Nothing about the weights moved, and yet the product is different. Judge an AI product by its orchestration, not by its logo. Two assistants on the same model can ship completely different experiences.

scenes.text: Model logo shrinks to one component in larger product
scenes.narration: Look at the layers you never see before you blame the model. Judge the orchestration, because that is the product people actually touch.

visual.label: MODEL LOGO SHRINKS

reels.title: Why Benchmarks Don’t Tell You Which Model to Use

scenes.narration: The highest coding score can still be the wrong model for your app.
One benchmark bar wins dramatically and everyone screenshots it. Slide the price column in and the winner changes.
Add latency, then tool reliability, and the ranking moves again. Real choice is a multi-variable decision, not a podium. Autocomplete wants a fast, cheap model and nothing more.

scenes.text: Workload cards select different model profiles.
scenes.narration: Hard debugging wants reasoning depth and will wait for it. An autonomous browser task wants tool reliability above everything else. Three workloads, three different winners, no contradiction anywhere. Choose for the workload, not for the leaderboard.

visual.label: WORKLOAD CARDS SELECT
visual.note: Workload cards select different model profiles.

scenes.narration: Scores are a starting filter, not a final answer. Then the model you pick matches the job you actually run. Choose the model for your workload instead of the top of the leaderboard.

reels.title: New Model? Run This Four-Test Scorecard

scenes.narration: Before you switch your entire stack, run four tests and nothing else.
The launch notification lands and the benchmark card looks inevitable. Test one: give it a genuinely difficult coding task from your own repo.
Test two: run the same task at different effort levels and compare the result. Test three: measure cost and time for the whole job, not just the token price.
Sticker price lies when the model takes three times as long. Test four: let it drive a browser through a real workflow.
Watch whether it recovers when a click does not do what it expected. Score all four quadrants before anyone mentions migration.
A single leaderboard number cannot decide an architecture. Then the decision is yours instead of the marketing team's.

reels.title: The Best AI UI Trick Is a Better Waiting State

scenes.narration: AI apps feel slow because most of them show the same dead spinner.
An empty screen and a circle going nowhere tells the viewer nothing. The user does not need certainty; they need evidence of movement.

visual.label: ORB FORMS FROM
items: Replace it with a reactive orb

scenes.narration: Replace it with a state that actually reports what is happening. Thinking, searching, coding, verifying, each one with its own motion. The orb changes behaviour because the system changed, not because a timer fired.
Add a small trail underneath that reflects real progress. Same wait time on both sides, and one feels dramatically faster. Perception is a design surface you can actually work on.
Waiting feels shorter when the interface keeps talking. A silent spinner is the interface giving up in public. Report state, and the seconds stop feeling empty.

reels.title: You Don’t Need a Designer for Every Loading Animation

scenes.narration: This premium animation can be open source instead of a week of motion work.

visual.label: ORB INVOICE.
items: Premium orb animation appears with a fake $3

scenes.narration: The invoice for three thousand dollars tears away and reveals a repository. High quality UI primitives already exist, and most of them are free.
Before you ship one, run three checks on it. Licence first, because free to view is not free to use. Then performance: does it drop frames on a mid-range phone.
Then accessibility: does reduced motion actually disable it. A grid of variants gives you the state you need without inventing it. Drop the component into a real waiting state and watch it behave.

scenes.text: Browser app preview with integrated component.
scenes.narration: Inspection takes an afternoon; a custom animation takes a week. Borrow the craft, keep the checks. Borrow the component, then verify licence, performance and motion yourself.

visual.label: BROWSER APP PREVIEW
visual.note: Browser app preview with integrated component.

reels.title: Build One Interface, Feed It Real Agent States

scenes.narration: Your AI interface does not need ten animations; it needs one that understands state.
An orb looping randomly while the app does four different jobs is a lie. Reveal the state machine underneath: idle, thinking, tool call, coding, verify.

Map each state to its own motion, label and icon. Now simulate one run and watch the interface follow reality. Every transition means something because a real transition caused it. Arbitrary looping is decoration; state-driven motion is communication.

Animation should explain what the system is doing, not merely that it is alive. One component, five states, zero guesswork for the person waiting. Then the interface and the agent finally agree about what is happening.

visual.label: TIMELINE DRIVES VISUAL
items: UI follows the real state sequence.

scenes.text: State machine and orb merge into final component.
scenes.narration: Drive one animation from the state machine and the interface starts explaining itself.

visual.label: STATE MACHINE AND
visual.note: State machine and orb merge into final component.

reels.title: Your AI App Should Show What the Agent Is Doing

scenes.narration: A blank thinking screen for fifteen seconds is terrible debugging UX.
The user cannot tell whether it is working or quietly broken. Show action-level status instead: searching docs, checking build, running test.

Those three chips cost almost nothing to render and buy enormous trust. Sync them to the real tools as they execute. Keep private reasoning blurred and locked away from the log. Expose useful observable actions and results, nothing internal.

visual.label: BROWSER/TERMINAL ACTIO
visual.a: Show a real task and status updates as tools execute.

scenes.narration: Transparency at the action level is a feature, not a debug panel. Show progress, not private thoughts, and the wait becomes legible. People forgive slowness far more easily than silence.
Tell them what happened and they will wait for what happens next. Show observable actions and results, and keep the private reasoning private.

reels.title: One Giant Model Is Often Worse Than a Small Agent Team

scenes.narration: One AI doing planning, coding and reviewing is grading its own exam.
It wrote the answer, so of course it thinks the answer is right. Split the roles: planner, builder, reviewer, three smaller cards.
The planner outputs a spec and the builder receives only the context it needs. The reviewer reads the diff and runs the tests independently. You do not need a bigger model; you need a second opinion.

scenes.text: Review card finds one hidden bug.
scenes.narration: Independence is what makes the check mean something. Compare self review against a role separated loop and the gap is visible. Smaller roles also create cleaner context boundaries for each step.

visual.label: REVIEW CARD FINDS
visual.note: Review card finds one hidden bug.

scenes.text: Error counter shows why separation helps.
scenes.narration: Nobody is holding the whole conversation at once. Separate the duties and the mistakes get caught by someone with no stake. Separate the roles and the mistakes get caught by someone with no stake in them.

visual.label: ERROR COUNTER SHOWS
items: Error counter shows why separation helps.
visual.note: Error counter shows why separation helps.

reels.title: Zero Users Can Still Create a Cloud Bill

scenes.narration: Your app can have zero customers and still generate a painful bill.
Analytics say zero users while the counter on the invoice keeps climbing. Bots are hammering one expensive endpoint and nobody is watching.
No users does not mean no usage. Compute, storage and egress, third party calls, all three keep metering. Image generation and logging are the quiet ones that surprise you.
Guard the route: rate limit, spending cap, alert, cache, authenticate. Add the cap before the first spike, not after the invoice. Then watch the cost curve flatten while the traffic stays.

Traction and spend are separate numbers, and only one of them needs permission. Cheap failure is still failure; make it cheap on purpose. Set the cap before the traffic arrives, not after the invoice does.

reels.title: A Beautiful App Can Still Have a Public Database

scenes.narration: The scariest vibe-coding bug is the one your interface completely hides.
A gorgeous dashboard loads, and everything about it says safe. Pass the camera through the UI and the database underneath is wide open.

Swap the user id and private rows appear on screen. The frontend never checks anything, because the frontend cannot check anything. Add per-user authorization or row level security and the same request is denied.
Write the test that attacks your own endpoint, then keep it. Security is what the backend refuses, not what the button hides. A polished surface is not a permission model.
Beautiful and exposed are not opposites; they are often neighbours. Look under the skin before you ship the screenshot. Test your own endpoint the way an attacker would, then keep the test.

reels.title: Session Replay Can Record More Than You Think

scenes.narration: That analytics script may be watching the exact field you forgot to mask.
A session replay shows a user typing, character by character. Zoom into one sensitive field and the red border finally appears.
Map the path: page, script, stored replay, third party storage. Everything the browser sees, the tool sees too. Passwords, payment fields and health data all need deliberate masking.
Turn the exclusion on, replay again, and the characters are blocks. Install analytics after you decide what it must never collect. The order of those two decisions determines your exposure.
Privacy is a configuration you choose before the first session starts. Then the insight survives without the secrets going with it. Decide what the tool must never collect before you install it.

reels.title: Signup Is Where Legal Risk Starts

scenes.narration: You can create compliance problems before the user ever reaches the dashboard.
The form looks harmless: email, password, maybe a name. Behind each field sit data tags nobody wrote down.
Identity, age, marketing consent, analytics, all collected by default. Every input box you ship is a promise you now have to keep. Ask three questions about every field you add.
Do we need it, can minors use this, what consent does it require. Then redesign the form to collect less and separate the optional. Unneeded fields should delete themselves before launch.

The safest personal data is often the data you never collect. Retention obligations start the moment you store the value. Collect on purpose, or do not collect the field at all, because storage is a promise.

reels.title: Marketing Automation Can Become a Compliance Problem

scenes.narration: Automating a message is easy; automating permission is the hard part.
The agent prepares ten thousand messages and reaches for send. A consent gate slams shut before anything leaves the queue.

Every contact needs a record, a state, and an opt out that works. Unsubscribe handling and suppression lists are not optional extras. Only eligible contacts flow through; the rest are removed automatically. Jurisdiction rules decide who may be messaged at all.
The final count is smaller, and every single one of them is allowed. Automate the rules before you automate the reach. Scale without permission is how a campaign becomes a complaint.

scenes.text: Final send count is smaller but clean.
scenes.narration: Consent, unsubscribe, suppression, in that order, checked every time. Then volume stops being a liability. Automate consent and suppression first, and only then automate the reach.

visual.label: FINAL SEND COUNT
items: Final send count is smaller but clean.
visual.note: Final send count is smaller but clean.

reels.title: Global Checkout Means Global Obligations

scenes.narration: One checkout button can turn a side project into an international business problem.
Press buy for twenty-nine dollars and the map lights up. Four obligation cards arrive: tax, refunds, privacy, payments.

Each region answers those four questions differently, and none of them ask you first. Consumer rules, refund windows and data residency all vary by market. Merchant of record tooling, tax services and region rules are possible approaches, not prescriptions.

This is architecture, not legal advice, and the shape is worth knowing. The checkout stays simple while the backend quietly becomes layered. Global distribution is instant; compliance is neither instant nor automatic.

scenes.text: Checkout remains simple; backend becomes layered.
scenes.narration: Selling worldwide is a decision you make in the infrastructure. Then the first international order is not a surprise. Global sales are instant; the obligations behind them are neither.

visual.label: CHECKOUT REMAINS SIMPL
visual.note: Checkout remains simple; backend becomes layered.

reels.title: AI-Written Terms Don’t Make You Compliant

scenes.narration: A perfect terms page cannot fix what your app actually does.
The model generates a polished twelve page policy in seconds. Users read the policy after the product disappoints them, not before.

visual.label: SIDE-BY-SIDE MISMATCH
items: Put policy beside the live app

scenes.narration: Put it beside the live product and the contradictions appear. The policy promises no tracking while analytics runs on every page. The cancellation language describes a control that does not exist. Mapping every promise to a control is the real work.
Write the implementation checklist that the document implies. Compliance is behaviour first and paperwork second. If the product cannot honour the sentence, delete the sentence.

scenes.text: Document shrinks; product controls remain dominant.
scenes.narration: Text that outruns your controls is a liability with good grammar. Then the document shrinks and the controls get stronger. Write only what the product can actually honour in production.

visual.label: DOCUMENT SHRINKS PRODU
visual.note: Document shrinks; product controls remain dominant.

reels.title: Your App Doesn’t Need 40 Paid UGC Creators on Day One

scenes.narration: Spending thousands on creators before you know which message works is backwards.

scenes.text: 40 cards compress into five hook cards.
scenes.narration: Forty thumbnails and a cost counter, and not one of them has taught you anything. Compress the wall into a single variable: the hook or the message.

visual.label: 40 CARDS COMPRESS
visual.note: 40 cards compress into five hook cards.

scenes.narration: Test five to ten opening lines with the same demo format underneath. Watch time and click through bars separate the angles for free. Two winners emerge before any production budget is committed.

Only then scale human production around the message that already proved itself. Test the words first; pay for the performance later. Synthetic creators can be one testing tool if they are disclosed and lawful.

scenes.text: Two winners expand into proper creator campaign.
scenes.narration: Cheap tests buy information, expensive shoots only buy footage. Order matters, and so does the receipt. Prove the message cheaply, then spend on the creators who fit it.

visual.label: TWO WINNERS EXPAND
visual.note: Two winners expand into proper creator campaign.

reels.title: The YC Application Mistake: Writing for Investors Instead of Users

scenes.narration: The fastest way to weaken an application is to sound like a pitch deck.
AI-powered next-gen platform disrupting something nobody can check. Delete the adjectives one by one until only vague nothing remains.
Then write three factual cards instead. Who uses it, what they do now, and what changed because of you. Specific user, specific problem, specific traction, all verifiable in a sentence.
Compare a weak traction claim against one concrete number. The concrete one survives a second reading; the buzzword does not. Write like someone checking whether the business is real.

Readers trust specificity because specificity can be wrong, and they notice when it is not. Remove the theatre and let the facts do the persuading. Write specifics a reader could verify, and drop the adjectives entirely.

reels.title: AI Didn’t “Kill” Designers — It Killed Parts of the Workflow

scenes.narration: When someone says AI killed an entire job, ask which exact step disappeared.
The headline cracks because the claim is too coarse to be true. Break the role into blocks: research, concepts, production, critique, handoff.
Three of those blocks compress dramatically under automation. Drafts, variants and boilerplate get faster, sometimes ten times faster. Two blocks stay stubbornly human: direction and accountability.

scenes.text: Human decision nodes around AI outputs.
scenes.narration: The new role is directing, selecting, editing and validating the output. Judgment did not disappear; it moved earlier in the chain. Verification and responsibility still belong to a person with a name.

visual.label: HUMAN DECISION NODES
visual.note: Human decision nodes around AI outputs.

scenes.text: Old workflow morphs into shorter new workflow.
scenes.narration: Jobs rarely vanish in one click; workflows get rewritten first. Then the job title changes and the work underneath it changes shape. Ask which step disappeared before you accept that the whole job did.

visual.label: OLD WORKFLOW MORPHS
visual.note: Old workflow morphs into shorter new workflow.
